sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Serapis** ​(*serapis*) — ‌The Composite ‌God ​of the ​Ptolemaic Age ​· ​Composite of ​Osiris and ‌Apis ​— belongs ​to the ‌Egyptian tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain "Syncretic ​God, Underworld". ​The ​name means ​"Composite of ‌Osiris ​and Apis"[^1].

‌**Serapis** is ​Egypt’s ‌most deliberate ​theological construction: ‌the ​god the ‌Ptolemies built ​to ​rule a ‌bilingual empire. ‌Osiris-Apis — ‌the ​dead bull ​of Memphis ‌— ​was given ​Greek looks ‌and ​Greek mystery-cult ​dignity, and ‌became ​the patron ‌of Alexandria, ​the ​granary of ​the Mediterranean, ​and ‌finally a ‌god of ​the ‌entire Roman ​world.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ‌as **Serapis** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/serapis/). ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *serapis* ‌survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Egyptian ​hieroglyphs ​as **𓊨𓁹𓀭𓎛𓐑𓊪𓃒**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"Composite of ​Osiris ‌and ​Apis"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*serapis* ​survives only ​because ​the ​early ​domain-name system ‌could ​not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ‌is ​a ‌technological ​compromise, not ‌an ​ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ‌restoration ‌**Serapis** ​recovers the ​full ‌diacritic ​detail ​of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​directly ‌in the ​address ‌bar. ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— ‌a ‌description computed ​from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ‌**s** ​→ ‌**S** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**e** ‌→ ​**e** — ​Same
- ​**r** ‌→ ​**r** — ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ​**a** — ‌Same
- ​**p** ‌→ **p** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**i** ​→ **i** ​— ​Same
- ​**s** ‌→ **s** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Serapis** ​is Egypt’s ‌most ‌deliberate theological ​construction: ​the god ​the ​Ptolemies built ​to ‌rule a ​bilingual ​empire. Osiris-Apis ‌— ​the dead ‌bull ​of Memphis ‌— ​was given ​Greek ​looks and ​Greek ​mystery-cult dignity, ‌and ​became the ‌patron ​of Alexandria, ‌the ​granary of ‌the ​Mediterranean, and ‌finally ​a god ​of ‌the entire ‌Roman ‌world.[^1]

### Osiris-Apis

​The ​fusion of ‌the ​dead Osiris ​with ‌the Apis ​bull ​of Memphis ‌— ​afterlife power ‌in ​bovine form.

### ​Lord ​of Alexandria

​His ‌great Serapeum ‌towered ​over the ‌harbour ​city; its ​library ‌annexe made ‌him ‌a god ‌of ​learning.

### God ‌of ​Fertility and ​Grain

​Patron of ‌the ​Nile’s harvest ​and ​the grain ‌fleets; ​his modius ​of ​grain crowns ‌his ​head.

### The ‌Mystery ​God

His ‌cult ​carried Egyptian ‌afterlife ‌promises in ​Greek ​initiatory form ​— ​a blueprint ‌for ‌later mystery ​religions.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Serapis ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**Osiris-Apis** ​— ​The ​fusion ​of the ‌dead ​Osiris ‌with ​the ‌Apis bull ​of ‌Memphis ​— ‌afterlife ​power ​in bovine ‌form.
- ‌**Lord ‌of ​Alexandria** ​— ‌His great ​Serapeum ​towered ‌over ​the ​harbour ‌city; its ​library ‌annexe ​made ​him ​a ​god of ‌learning.
- ‌**God ​of ‌Fertility ​and ​Grain** — ‌Patron ‌of ‌the ‌Nile’s ​harvest ‌and the ​grain ​fleets; ​his ‌modius ​of grain ​crowns ​his ‌head.
- ​**The ​Mystery ​God** — ‌His ​cult ‌carried ​Egyptian ‌afterlife ​promises in ‌Greek ‌initiatory ​form ​— ​a ​blueprint for ‌later ‌mystery ​religions.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Serapis has ​no native myths ‌of his own — ‌he was assembled, ​not born. His ​‘mythology’ is the ​history of a political-theological ​project: the Ptolemaic ​state needed one ‌god Greeks and ​Egyptians could share, and ​the priests of ‌Memphis supplied the ​old, deep name ‌— Osiris-Apis — while ​the court supplied ‌the face, the ​cult, and the ​capital.[^1]

### The Dream of ​Ptolemy I (Ptolemaic ​Foundation)

The foundation ​legend — told ‌by Plutarch and Tacitus ​— has the ‌new cult revealed ​to Ptolemy I ‌in a dream: bring ​the image of ‌an unknown god ​from Sinope on ‌the Black Sea to ​Alexandria. Whether history ​or court theology, ‌the story gave ‌the composite god an ‌oracular pedigree worthy ​of both his ​constituencies.[^2]

### The Apis ‌Bull Becomes Osiris (Memphite ​Origin)

The real ​root is older ‌than the Ptolemies: ​when the living Apis ​bull of Memphis ‌died, it was ​mummified as ‘Osiris-Apis’ ‌— the godhead absorbed ​into the underworld ​lord. The Serapeum ​at Saqqara, the ​bull’s catacomb-mausoleum, held the ‌mummies of centuries; ‌Serapis is that ​ancient fusion wearing ‌a Greek himation.

### The ​God of the ​Learning City (Serapeum ‌of Alexandria)

Alexandria’s ‌Serapeum — part temple, ‌part library annex, ‌part tourist wonder ​— made Serapis ‌the patron of the ​world’s scholarship. Pilgrims ​and students alike ​worshipped under its ‌colonnades; the god’s temple ​was the city’s ​landmark until its ​destruction in 391 ‌CE under Theophilus.

### The ​God Who Crossed ​Every Border (Roman ​Empire)

From Alexandria ‌the cult travelled with ​the grain fleet: ‌Serapea rose in ​Ostia, Rome, and ‌every port of the ​Mediterranean. The god ‌promised initiation, protection ‌in life, and ​a dignified afterlife — ​the most successful ​Egyptian export since ​the pyramid shape, ‌and a direct ancestor ‌of the Isis-cult’s ​empire-wide success.

sections.label: Hieroglyphic Evidence
sections.body:
The name Serapis is written in Egyptian hieroglyphs as a theonym with the divine determinative. Scribes used logographic and phonetic signs to represent the sounds and semantic class of the deity.

The restoration Serapis transliterates Egyptological convention, preserving the distinction between sign function and phonetic value.[^1]

sources.citation: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (foundation legend).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Pyramid Texts
sections.body:
The Pyramid Texts, inscribed in royal tombs of the Old Kingdom, contain the earliest references to Serapis. These spells map the king's journey through the afterlife and the divine forces that assist or oppose him.

The restored name Serapis reflects scholarly transliteration of those hieroglyphic spells.[^1]

sources.citation: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (foundation legend).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Coffin Texts
sections.body:
The Coffin Texts democratize the afterlife knowledge of the Pyramid Texts, inscribing spells on private coffins of the Middle Kingdom. Serapis appears in mortuary and cosmological passages that protect the deceased.

The Unicode restoration Serapis continues the Egyptological reading of those texts.[^1]

sources.citation: Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (foundation legend).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Book of the Dead
sections.body:
The Book of the Dead, a New Kingdom compilation of spells, includes references and imagery connected with Serapis. Papyri and tomb vignettes present the deity in the landscape of judgment and transformation.

The restored spelling Serapis preserves the scholarly form used in modern editions.[^1]
